title: Meridian: a dated processing example
disclosure: Synthetic interview — fictional company and speaker

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: What were the units and period in your Meridian processing example?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: In the fictional January 2026 example, processing revenue was USD 120,000 on 2,000,000 transactions.

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: The figures exclude refunds and are not annual revenue, profit or a forecast.

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: I have no figures for February 2026.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Can you describe the typical transaction types that contributed to the 2 million transactions in January 2026?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Certainly. The bulk were low-value retail purchases, mostly under USD 10, processed through point-of-sale terminals. There was also a smaller portion of online payments and some recurring subscription charges. The variety was broad, but retail dominated the volume.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Did you observe any seasonal or promotional factors influencing the transaction volume or revenue during that month?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: January typically sees a post-holiday dip, but in this case, there was a modest promotional campaign by a few merchants, which slightly boosted transaction counts. However, the average transaction value remained relatively stable, so revenue gains were modest compared to volume increases.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How was the data collected and verified for accuracy in your example?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Data was aggregated from multiple payment gateways feeding into Meridian's central ledger. Verification involved cross-checking transaction logs against settlement reports and flagging anomalies for manual review. Despite these controls, occasional discrepancies occurred, usually due to delayed refunds or chargebacks not yet reflected in the dataset.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: You mentioned refunds were excluded. How did that impact the interpretation of the revenue figure?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Excluding refunds means the revenue figure represents gross processing income before adjustments. This provides a snapshot of transaction activity but can overstate net revenue if refund rates are significant. In this example, refunds were relatively low, so the figure was a reasonable proxy for income generated.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Was there any notable variation in transaction volume or revenue across different merchant categories?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Yes, certain sectors like grocery and convenience stores showed consistent high volume with low average transaction values, while categories such as electronics had fewer transactions but higher ticket sizes. This diversity affected overall revenue patterns but was typical for the processing environment at that time.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Did you have any insight into how these figures compared to previous months or years?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Unfortunately, I did not have access to comparable data from earlier periods, so I could not establish trends or growth rates. The January 2026 snapshot was isolated, limiting broader analysis.
